result:
The rain had been falling for three days without pause, turning the narrow streets of the old quarter into shallow rivers that reflected the sodium lamps in long, trembling streaks. Elara stood at the window of her third-floor room, one palm pressed to the cold glass, watching a discarded newspaper sail past like a pale boat. She had not slept. The machine on the table behind her hummed at a frequency just below hearing, a soft electrical purr that made the hairs on her arms lift.

She had built it from salvaged parts: a cracked oscilloscope, copper coils wound by hand, a vacuum tube that still glowed cherry-red when the current ran true. The dream-catcher, she called it in the notebooks no one else would ever read. Not because she believed dreams could be netted like fish, but because the alternative—that the mind simply extinguished each night and reignited without memory of the dark—felt unbearable. If something persisted in that interval, she wanted to know its shape.

At dawn she fitted the sensors to her temples. The adhesive was cold. She lay back on the narrow cot, counted backward from one hundred, and let the machine take the first sample. When she woke, the rain had thinned to mist. On the screen a pale waveform stuttered, then resolved into a corridor of doors, each one slightly ajar. She recognized none of them. Behind the third door a woman who looked like her mother, only younger, was folding paper cranes and setting them on a windowsill. The cranes did not stay. One by one they lifted, beat wings of creased newsprint, and vanished into a sky the color of weak tea. Elara watched until the image dissolved into static. Her hands were shaking.

She ran the recording again, slower. The woman’s mouth moved. No sound, only the shape of words. Elara leaned closer, trying to read them. Something about a key. Something about not forgetting the blue door at the end. She paused the frame, sketched the doorway in her notebook, then went downstairs to buy coffee she could not afford.

The café on the corner still had power. The owner, a man with a scar like a question mark across his knuckles, poured her a cup and did not ask why her eyes were red. She sat by the window and drew the blue door from memory until the lines blurred. When she returned to the room the machine had cooled. She rewound the coils, replaced a fuse that had blackened, and lay down again before the light failed completely.

This time the corridor was longer. The doors were numbered in a script she almost understood. Behind one, a child version of herself sat on a linoleum floor sorting buttons by color. The child looked up, unsurprised, and held out a single blue button the size of a coin. Elara reached for it in the dream and woke with her fingers closed on nothing. The waveform on the screen showed a sharp spike at the moment of contact, then flatlined. She labeled the file “Button” and stored it beside the others.

By the fifth night the rain had stopped. The streets steamed. Elara no longer needed the adhesive; the sensors clung by static alone. She had begun to leave the machine running while she was awake, letting it sample the ordinary drift of thought. Most of what it captured was noise—grocery lists, half-remembered songs, the particular squeak of the stair that meant the neighbor was home. Once, though, it caught a fragment that did not belong to her: a man standing in an orchard at night, counting the fruit by touch because the moon was gone. He wore her father’s coat. When she tried to follow him between the trees the image tore, and she found herself staring at the water stain on her ceiling, heart loud in her ears.

She started leaving the window open. Moths came in, drawn to the vacuum tube’s glow, and died against the glass with soft, final taps. Elara swept them into a jar and labeled that, too. Evidence, she told herself. Of what, she did not say.

On the eighth night the corridor ended. The blue door stood at the far end, paint peeling in long curls. She pushed it open. Beyond was the room she was lying in, exactly as it was, except the cot was empty and the machine on the table had been dismantled, its parts arranged in a careful spiral. In the center of the spiral sat the blue button. She picked it up. It was warm. When she turned it over, a single word had been scratched into the plastic on the reverse side, so small she had to bring it to her eye: Stay.

She woke with the button still in her hand. It was real. The plastic had a hairline crack and smelled faintly of the adhesive she used on the sensors. For a long time she did not move. The machine hummed. Outside, someone was sweeping the street, the broom making a dry, rhythmic sound against wet stone. Elara set the button on the table beside the coils. She did not label it. She opened her notebook to a fresh page, wrote the date, and then, beneath it, the only sentence that seemed accurate: The door was already open.

She stayed awake until the light returned, watching the button and listening to the ordinary noises of the building—the pipes, the neighbor’s radio, a dog barking three streets away. When the first cart rattled past below, she rose, washed her face, and began, very carefully, to take the machine apart. Each coil she unwound and laid in a straight line. Each tube she wrapped in cloth. The oscilloscope she returned to the shelf where she had found it months ago, its screen dark. By noon the table was clear except for the button and the notebook. She closed the notebook, slid it into the drawer, and went downstairs to see whether the café still had coffee. The owner looked at her hands, empty now, and poured the cup without speaking. She drank it slowly, watching the street dry in the sun, and did not think about doors.
